params.question: Provoked seizures, such as those caused by hypoglycaemia or alcohol withdrawal, count towards a diagnosis of epilepsy under the ILAE 2014 criteria.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Not quite. Provoked seizures do not count towards a diagnosis of epilepsy. The ILAE 2014 criteria specifically require unprovoked seizures. When a reversible cause like hypoglycaemia or alcohol withdrawal is identified, the treatment is to address that cause — antiepileptic drugs are not indicated.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. The ILAE 2014 definition requires unprovoked seizures — two or more separated by at least 24 hours, one with at least 60% recurrence risk, or a recognised epilepsy syndrome. Provoked seizures have a reversible cause and need cause-directed treatment, not antiepileptic drugs.

params.question: A 28-year-old man has a first unprovoked generalised tonic-clonic seizure. His acute metabolic screen is entirely normal. An EEG performed the next day shows no epileptiform discharges. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Reassure the patient that epilepsy has been excluded and discharge without follow-up

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A normal EEG does not exclude epilepsy. Further investigation, including neuroimaging, is essential before any conclusion can be drawn.

answers.text: Start carbamazepine empirically to prevent a second seizure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Starting medication after a single seizure without completing the three-tier investigation is premature. The workup must be completed before treatment decisions are made.

answers.text: Arrange an MRI brain with epilepsy protocol and consider repeating the EEG after sleep deprivation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A normal EEG does not exclude epilepsy — sleep deprivation and photic stimulation improve the diagnostic yield. MRI with the epilepsy protocol (thin coronal FLAIR cuts through the hippocampi) completes the three-tier investigation framework.

answers.text: Perform an urgent lumbar puncture to rule out central nervous system infection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Lumbar puncture is indicated only when CNS infection is suspected. In the absence of fever, meningism, or immunocompromise, it is not part of the routine first-seizure workup.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the three-tier investigation: acute metabolic screen, EEG (a normal result does not exclude epilepsy), and neuroimaging with MRI epilepsy protocol. Complete all tiers before making treatment decisions.
Well done. Completing the three-tier investigation — metabolic screen, EEG, and neuroimaging — is essential before reaching a diagnosis or starting treatment.

interactions.label: A patient has been seizing continuously for 25 minutes. Intravenous lorazepam wa

params.question: A patient has been seizing continuously for 25 minutes. Intravenous lorazepam was given at 7 minutes and repeated at 12 minutes with no response. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Give a third dose of intravenous lorazepam

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: After two benzodiazepine doses, repeating a third is unlikely to succeed. Progressive GABA-A receptor internalisation reduces benzodiazepine efficacy the longer a seizure continues.

Correct. In the 20–40 minute window, after benzodiazepine failure, the protocol calls for a second-line intravenous AED. Delaying this transition is the most common error in status epilepticus management.

answers.text: Intubate and start a propofol or thiopentone infusion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Anaesthetic infusions are reserved for refractory status epilepticus — seizures persisting beyond 40 minutes despite first- and second-line agents. At 25 minutes, second-line AEDs should be tried first.

Intramuscular midazolam is a first-line alternative when IV access is unavailable. This patient already has IV access and has failed two benzodiazepine doses — switching to a different benzodiazepine is unlikely to help.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the timed status epilepticus protocol: 0–5 min ABC and glucose, 5–20 min IV lorazepam or IM midazolam, 20–40 min second-line IV AED (levetiracetam, valproate, or phenytoin), beyond 40 min ICU with anaesthetic infusion.
Excellent. The timed protocol is: benzodiazepines first (5–20 min), second-line IV AEDs next (20–40 min), and ICU anaesthetic infusions if refractory (beyond 40 min).

params.question: A 26-year-old woman with epilepsy well-controlled on sodium valproate wishes to plan a pregnancy. What is the most appropriate advice?

answers.text: Continue sodium valproate and add standard-dose folic acid at 400 micrograms daily

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Sodium valproate is the most teratogenic AED, causing neural tube defects. Standard-dose folic acid alone does not adequately compensate for this risk. The drug must be switched before conception.

answers.text: Stop all antiepileptic medication immediately to protect the foetus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Abruptly stopping AEDs risks breakthrough seizures and status epilepticus, which are dangerous for both the mother and the foetus. A planned switch to a safer drug is the correct approach.

answers.text: Switch to lamotrigine or levetiracetam before conception and start high-dose folic acid

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Sodium valproate causes neural tube defects and is the most important AED safety concern in women of childbearing age. Switching to lamotrigine or levetiracetam and starting high-dose folic acid before planned conception is the standard of care.

answers.text: Delay pregnancy until she has been seizure-free and off all medication for at least two years

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pregnancy is not contraindicated in women with epilepsy. Many women can safely carry a pregnancy on appropriate AEDs. The key is switching away from valproate to a safer alternative before conception.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: sodium valproate causes neural tube defects and must be switched to a safer AED (lamotrigine or levetiracetam) before a planned pregnancy. High-dose folic acid should also be started.
Well done. Valproate teratogenicity is the most important AED safety issue in reproductive-age women. Pre-conception planning with drug switching and high-dose folic acid is essential.
